research_question: How effective are LLM-based agents at automating systematic literature reviews?

sub_questions.text: What approaches and architectures are used for llm-based agents automating systematic literature reviews?

selected_papers.title: Hallucinated references and citation errors in LLM-generated literature reviews
selected_papers.abstract: Large language models can fabricate references or corrupt citation details. We analyse limitations and risks of LLM-based agents automating systematic literature reviews, finding that ungrounded generation produced non-existent DOIs and mismatched metadata, while agents retrieving from scholarly indexes and verifying DOIs reduced these errors substantially.

selected_papers.title: Multi-agent architectures for automating systematic literature reviews
selected_papers.abstract: We describe a multi-agent architecture in which LLM-based agents plan search strategies, screen titles and abstracts, and draft evidence tables for systematic literature reviews. A deterministic controller coordinates the agents and enforces review protocol rules. Methods for decomposing review questions into search queries are compared across three domains.

selected_papers.title: Evaluating LLM-based agents for title and abstract screening in systematic reviews
selected_papers.abstract: This evaluation measures how accurately LLM-based agents screen titles and abstracts for systematic literature reviews. Across four review datasets the agents reached high recall but variable precision, and performance depended strongly on prompt design. We report evaluation metrics, error categories and the human effort saved by automating the screening stage.

selected_papers.title: Human oversight in semi-automated systematic reviews
selected_papers.abstract: Semi-automated tools for systematic literature reviews keep humans responsible for final inclusion decisions. This study examines limitations of automating review stages with LLM-based agents, including automation bias and reduced reviewer attention, and proposes checkpoints at which human reviewers approve agent outputs before the workflow continues.

selected_papers.title: Reproducibility limitations of language-model screening in evidence reviews
selected_papers.abstract: Language-model outputs vary between runs and model versions. We test the reproducibility of LLM-based agents automating systematic literature reviews and find that screening decisions changed for a notable share of records across repeated runs, a limitation that requires logging prompts, model versions and decisions for audit.

selected_papers.title: Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines for literature review automation
selected_papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds language model outputs in retrieved documents. We present methods for building retrieval pipelines that support automating systematic literature reviews, including query expansion, abstract retrieval and citation linking, and discuss architectures that keep generated summaries traceable to sources.

selected_papers.title: Planning and tool use in LLM-based research agents
selected_papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly plan multi-step research tasks and call external tools such as scholarly search engines. This paper surveys planning methods, including task decomposition and reflection, and analyses how agents for automating literature reviews select tools, recover from failed searches and record their decisions for audit.

selected_papers.title: Comparative evaluation of agentic and single-prompt approaches to literature reviews
selected_papers.abstract: We compare agentic workflows with single-prompt baselines for automating systematic literature reviews. In an evaluation on twelve review topics, agentic workflows improved recall of relevant studies but increased cost and latency, and gains depended on the task and the coordination architecture.

selected_papers.title: Benchmarking automated evidence synthesis with large language models
selected_papers.abstract: We benchmark large language models on evidence synthesis tasks drawn from published systematic literature reviews. Evaluation covers data extraction, summary faithfulness and agreement with human reviewers. Models performed well on extraction but produced unfaithful statements in a minority of summaries, which indicates that automating synthesis still requires human verification.
